name: Audience-Reactive Installations
title: Audience-Reactive Installations
answer: Audience-reactive installations are artworks that sense the people in the room and change what they show, play or do in response. They sit between interactive art, performance and experience design, and they usually run continuously rather than as a fixed show with a start and an end. The audience is not a viewer of a finished object but a participant whose movement, sound, touch or presence becomes part of the work. Typical settings include galleries, museums, festivals, public squares and commercial spaces.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The physical layer is sensors, cameras, microphones, depth trackers, pressure mats and touch surfaces, feeding a computer that decides what happens next. Output goes to projectors, LED walls, speakers, motors, lights or robotic elements, often through a media server or a game engine such as Unity or TouchDesigner. Because these works run unattended for hours or months, reliability matters as much as the effect: machines are usually locked down, auto-restarting and monitored remotely. Where the piece generates imagery, video or sound on the fly, it draws on the same model families the wider field uses, and this site tracks 1,000 live image generation models, 1,000 video models and 2,000 audio models among the tools available.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with observation: watching how people actually move through a space, then designing a loop of sensing, interpretation and response that reads clearly without instruction. Artists prototype with mock sensors and recorded footage before committing to a venue, then tune thresholds so the piece reacts to intent rather than to every passing shadow. Machine learning is often used for pose estimation, gesture classification, voice detection or generative output, while simpler rule-based logic handles timing and state. Teams are usually small and mixed, pairing an artist with a creative technologist, a fabricator and sometimes a sound designer, and the piece is rarely finished until it has survived a real public.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Reactive installations collect data about bodies and voices, which brings privacy duties even when nothing is stored: signage, consent where required, and defaults that discard raw sensor feeds are common practice. Copyright and licensing questions arise for generated images, video and music, and the field is watching how these disputes resolve, with 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site, 18 of them involving AI music services. Provenance is handled through documentation of models, datasets and versions, plus credits for collaborators, performers and any sampled material. Accessibility, child safety and the risk of capturing bystanders who never opted in are treated as design constraints, not afterthoughts.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward installations that recognise returning visitors, adapt over weeks rather than seconds, and share learned behaviour across a venue or a touring show. Cheaper depth sensing and on-device inference are moving heavy processing out of the back room and into the room itself, which changes what can be promised to a venue. At the same time, artists are pushing back on purely generative spectacle, favouring pieces where the model is one component among many and the audience relationship stays legible. Expect more emphasis on consent, on documented provenance for generated material, and on works that can be shown, stored and re-staged years after the original hardware is gone.
